# Storyboard: Chapter 5, Riffle’s River

*Generated by `tools/storyboard.mjs` from `app/story/ch05.js`. Do not edit by hand: change the story file and run `node tools/storyboard.mjs` again.*

## How to read this

Every screen of the game is one comic panel, called a frame. Frames are listed in reading order. Each one has:

- **Shot**: the storyboard, written for an illustrator (camera, who is where, what the moment feels like, where the lettering goes).
- **Scene**: what the game draws today, in plain words: the set, the camera, who is in shot and how, and any effects.
- **Captions**: the narration boxes, read first. **Balloons**: who speaks, in order. **Sound effect**: the big lettering. A line marked *(only if …)* shows only to a reader whose choices match.
- **Then**: what the reader does next (tap Next, choose, type, pick a look, count by twos, or do a Counts lesson).

Where the reader makes a choice, each option’s frames are grouped under a **Branch** heading, and the branches meet again at the frame named after them. `{name}` is the first part of her Clan name (Moon makes Moonpaw), `{petname}` is what her Tall One calls her, and `{they}`/`{them}`/`{their}` become she/her/her or he/him/his. `{Murmur}`/`{murmur}` is the tortoiseshell’s name word: Murmur (Murmurpaw, Murmurchime, murmuring), or Mutter for a reader whose own Clan name is Murmur.

## The chapter

### f001 · panel 1

**Shot.** WIDE, FROM THE FRONT, SUNRISE, THE TAP PICTURE. The prey pile in its rows under the bramble arch in the first gold light, the back row only a dark band in the brambles’ shadow, and at the front the grizzled old tom sitting as straight as a post with his eyes shut, a snail halfway up one ear. Our cat and Tallyheart have just come up on the other side. In play his nose glows softly; a tap on it makes his whiskers jump and the snail pull in its horns, and turns the page, and a tap anywhere else only makes him snore again. Captions top left; the snore lettered over his head.

**Scene.** Pile: the prey pile in camp, a shady corner under an arch of brambles, the fountain’s edge at the right, in the morning (mice and voles, soft and round with their tails tucked in, all eyes shut, laid out in rows). Camera: from the front: the rows running back under the brambles (`rows`). Cast: Tallyheart (walking, kind, in the crowd, facing left); you (standing, full of wonder, lying beside the pile, facing left); the grizzled old tom (sitting, sleepy, left of the pile, facing right, eyes shut: asleep sitting up, a snail halfway up one ear). Also: four rows of ten, running back under the brambles; the back row has four empty places side by side, right in its middle (three pieces, the gap, three pieces); the back row is a dark band in the brambles’ shadow: no gap, no dug earth and no “scale” can be made out; the “scale” where it was found, on the bare earth behind the back row: a small glint under the brambles. Effects: morning light, washed clean after the storm.

**Captions**

> At sunrise, the old tom sits by the prey pile, as straight as a post. He’s guarding.
>
> He’s guarding with his eyes shut. A snail is halfway up his ear.

**Sound effect:** SNNNRRRK.

**Then she taps the old tom’s nose** (one tap, on this scene): it glows softly; a tap on it turns the page to f002; a tap anywhere else gets a small answer (lettered small beside it: “snnnrrk…”) and nothing more. Nothing can be got wrong, and nothing is logged. The instruction under the panel: “Tap his nose to wake him up.” For VoiceOver, a hidden button: “Wake him up.”

**Then the Counts lesson** `ch05-nines` (lives): 2 × 9 (its own cats in the picture; its own lines after a right answer; its own lines after a right retry), 9 × 10 (its own question, kept on its retry; its own lines after a right answer; its own lines after a right retry), 4 × 9 (its own question, kept on its retry; its own lines after a right answer; its own lines after a right retry; its own lines after a miss; her answers scratched in the sand with its line), 9 × 1, 9 × 6 (its own question, kept on its retry; its own lines after a right answer; its own lines after a right retry), 3 × 9, 9 × 8, 5 × 9, 7 × 9, 9 × 9 (its own lines after a right answer; its own lines after a right retry). Every question it asks first, and every retry, plays the two steps in its picture without a word: all ten claws lit on every cat (the hop), one curling in on each (the tuck), then unlit, and she types. A question lent to fill a gap shows the still picture. She types each answer on the keypad; a miss gets the sand count in two steps (two swipes for every cat, hopped by tens; then one line rubbed out of every pair, stepping back by ones) and comes back two questions later (the questions in between are the easiest of her right answers in this lesson, not the latest). On to f018.

- After 2 × 9, right on its retry:
  - **Tallyheart**: “Eighteen! One and eight. There’s your nine.”
- Asking 9 × 10:
  - **Tallyheart**: “Ten cats. Ten tens make a hundred. Now tuck ten in.”
- Asking 9 × 10 again after a miss:
  - **Tallyheart**: “Here’s that one again. Ten cats. Ten tens make a hundred. Now tuck ten in.”
- After 9 × 10, right the first time:
  - **Tallyheart**: “Ninety! Yesterday it was nine cats, ten claws each. Same ninety!”
- After 9 × 10, right on its retry:
  - **Tallyheart**: “Ninety! Yesterday it was nine cats, ten claws each. Same ninety!”
- Asking 4 × 9:
  - **Tallyheart**: “Four cats. Hop by tens. Then tuck four in.”
- Asking 4 × 9 again after a miss:
  - **Tallyheart**: “Here’s that one again. Four cats. Hop by tens. Then tuck four in.”
- After 4 × 9, right the first time:
  - **Tallyheart**: “Thirty-six! Now look. Three and six make nine. {also}Every nines answer hides a nine!”
- After 4 × 9, right on its retry:
  - **Tallyheart**: “Thirty-six! Three and six. There’s your nine.”
- After a miss on 4 × 9, when it comes back:
  - **Tallyheart**: “Thirty-six. Now look. Three and six make nine. {also}Every nines answer hides a nine! We’ll come back to that one.”
- After a miss on 4 × 9, when it does not:
  - **Tallyheart**: “Thirty-six. Now look. Three and six make nine. {also}Every nines answer hides a nine!”
- With the lines after 4 × 9, right the first time or missed: her answers scratched in the sand, 18 and 36 (2 × 9 only once she has answered it right with no ask of it still to come; `{also}` in those lines is “One and eight make nine.” when they are all there, and nothing when not).
- Asking 9 × 6:

- Asking 9 × 6 again after a miss:
  - **Tallyheart**: “Here’s that one again. Six cats. Six tens make sixty. Now tuck six in.”
- After 9 × 6, right the first time:
  - **Tallyheart**: “Fifty-four! Five and four. There’s your nine.”
- After 9 × 6, right on its retry:
  - **Tallyheart**: “Fifty-four! Five and four. There’s your nine.”
- After 9 × 9, right the first time:
  - **Tallyheart**: “EIGHTY-ONE!”
  - **Murmurchime**: “Not mice.”
- After 9 × 9, right on its retry:
  - **Tallyheart**: “EIGHTY-ONE!”
  - **Murmurchime**: “Not mice.”
- After a miss that is the tens (the hop without the tuck): “That’s the hop! Now the tuck: one claw in for every cat.”
- After a miss that is the tens less one (one claw tucked, for two cats or more): “So close! You tucked ONE claw. Tuck one in for every cat.”
- After a miss whose two numbers don’t make nine, once the lesson has shown her that they should (in the Training Hollow, always): “Remember: the two numbers in a nines answer make nine. Let’s scratch it out together.”

- At the end: “That’s the nines.”

**Then the Counts lesson** `ch05-wisp` (legs in the water, little herons scratched in the mud): 7 × 1 (its own question, kept on its retry; its own lines after a right answer; its own lines after a right retry). She types each answer on the keypad; a miss gets the set’s own picture lit a group at a time, the player keeping the count, and comes back two questions later (the questions in between come from `ch01-tails`, the easiest first, never a pair asked already while there is another, each asked as this lesson’s own question, in its picture and its voice after “She draws another one.”). On to f106a.

- Asking 7 × 1:
  - *Caption*: Seven herons, each standing on one leg. How many legs in the water?
- Asking 7 × 1 again after a miss:
  - *Caption*: She taps the seven herons again.
  - *Caption*: Seven herons, each standing on one leg. How many legs in the water?
- After 7 × 1, right the first time:
  - *Caption*: She nods. Once.
- After 7 × 1, right on its retry:
  - *Caption*: She nods. Once.
- Before a question comes back: “She taps the seven herons again.”
- The help’s first line is said by Patience: “Look again. One leg each.”
- Nobody speaks in this set: every line the engine words itself (the question, a retry’s opening, the lines after a miss) is lettered as a caption.
- No closing line: the next frame goes straight on.

## The Case File’s cards

A piece of bark for each thing she finds out: one picture scratched in, one line, and a mark in a corner (an eye for what she saw herself, an ear for what she was only told). Each goes into her Case File at the panel that gives it, in this order:

| Card | Mark | Its line | Given at | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `prints-pile` | eye | Tiny prints in the dug earth behind the pile. | f005 |  |
| `puddle-paws` | ear | Puddle says clever little paws picked up mice on the storm night. | f064a, f129a | her file shows it only once foundPuddle is true |
| `otter-fox` | ear | The old otter says the fox told him the dragon story. | f069a, f134 |  |
| `fur` | eye | Thin brown fur at the Crossing. Not cat. Not otter. Not fox. | f074a, f139 |  |
| `heron-no-moon` | ear | Patience says there was NO moon on the storm night. | f084 | drawn touching `fox-moon` from the moment she holds both: “One of them is wrong.” |
| `heron-shapes` | ear | Patience says two small shapes crossed her mud, carrying something. | f088 | drawn touching `squall-shapes` from the moment she holds both: “Two saw them. The same two shapes?” |
| `prints-marsh` | eye | Tiny prints in the marsh mud. Much smaller than a cat’s. | f091, f092 | drawn touching `prints-pile` from the moment she holds both: “The same prints.” |
| `prints-tracks` | eye | The tiny prints run toward the train tracks. | f093 | drawn touching `squall-shapes` from the moment she holds both: “Both lead toward the tracks.” |
| `wisp-fox` | ear | Wisp drew a fox dropping something glittering in the reeds. | f111a | her file shows it only once foundWisp is true |

## The book page

Title: *{name}paw’s First Moon*. This chapter’s page, under “Chapter 5: Riffle’s River”. Lines shown when their condition matches the reader’s choices:

- (always) On {name}paw’s fourth morning, the old tom was guarding the pile with his eyes shut and a snail on his ear, and four more pieces were gone: sixteen in four nights.
- (always) Tallyheart taught {name}paw {their} fifth Count, nine lives: a ten with one claw tucked in.
- (if ch5Roof is true) On the roof of {their} old tower, {they} found Squall, the littlest dragonet, who told {them} about two skinny shapes that go to the tracks every night.
- (always) {name}paw sat through the Roar, the apprentices’ courage test, on the otters’ raft, and did not move one of nine claws. Tallyheart counted.
- (if foundPuddle is true) Under the raft {they} found Puddle, who has four big feet and says he is a log. Puddle saw clever little paws picking up mice on the storm night.
- (always) The old ferry otter said the fox had told him the dragon story, twice, and showed {name}paw a tuft of thin brown fur.
- (always) Patience the heron said there was no moon on the storm night, and that two small shapes crossed her mud. There were tiny prints in it. It cost eighteen fish.
- (if foundWisp is true) {name}paw sat still until a pale reed blinked. It was Wisp, who stands on one leg like a heron, and drew a fox dropping something glittering in the reeds.
- (if not (ch5Roof is false or not set and foundPuddle is false or not set and foundWisp is false or not set)) Under the Old Bridge, Sprinkle lit a forepaw for everyone found so far. Mama’s count is coming back.
- (always) That night, Tallyheart said every warrior has sat through the Roar. She counted through hers, very loudly.
- (no dream typed) {name}paw’s dream that night floated off down the river.

**A dragonet page:** Puddle (`puddle`), found in this chapter by a reader whose foundPuddle is true (the page is there only then). Her book gains a page for Puddle (drawn his head out of the water, a small bump on it), with room for her own drawing, beside the clutch still to find (silhouettes, seven dragonets in all):

> Blue-grey, with feet much too big for him. He says he is a log.
>
> {name}paw found him under the otters’ ferry raft. Mama says: stay where you land.
>
> He says five, and then he sinks. He always pops up again. Five more claws, counted.

**A dragonet page:** Wisp (`wisp`), found in this chapter by a reader whose foundWisp is true (the page is there only then). Her book gains a page for Wisp (drawn standing on one leg among the reeds, her eyes open), with room for her own drawing, beside the clutch still to find (silhouettes, seven dragonets in all):

> So pale you can nearly see the reeds through her. She thinks she is a heron.
>
> {name}paw found her in Patience’s reeds, by keeping very, very still.
>
> She stands on one leg, and draws what she has seen. Five more claws, counted.
